01 / Start here

Get useful work out of AI

The five-minute version

Start with something you actually want finished: understand your spending, assess a business idea, improve a job application, or organize a folder you keep avoiding. Give the AI a useful outcome to work toward.

With suitable tools and access, an agent can inspect files, research, make changes, run calculations, and check its work. What your particular setup can do depends on the tools and information it can reach. Ask it to check access early and explain any missing piece.

Your main job is to make your intentions and preferences clear. The AI should help you do that by asking questions, explaining choices, and investigating facts. It should also do the work and provide evidence that the result holds up.

Start with the outcome

“Make this spreadsheet better” leaves plenty of room for interpretation. “Help me understand my monthly spending and find recurring charges” gives the AI a direction. You can start there even if you have no idea what the finished workbook should contain.

Add whatever you already know: who will use the result, where the information is, what bothers you about the current version, and anything that must stay unchanged. An existing example or reference is useful if you have one. You can also explain your preferences through questions.

Clear instructions help. They cannot prevent every reasoning mistake or missing fact, which is why checking belongs in the workflow too.

Make the AI interview you

For substantial work, ask it to clarify the task before making changes. It should inspect the available information and ask about choices only you can settle. If the file already contains the date range, it can read that. Whether you want work expenses mixed with personal spending is your decision.

Have it group independent questions together, up to ten per round. Follow-up questions should reflect your answers. If you don't understand a choice, ask for a plain explanation, the tradeoffs, and a recommendation. “I don't know” should lead to help deciding; it isn't permission to silently choose for you.

The interview ends when the decisions that matter are settled and you confirm the recap. Facts that still need investigation should be named, with a way to investigate them. This adapts the grilling workflow.

Approve a plan you can understand

Before substantial work begins, the AI should briefly explain the intended result, your key preferences, what it will change, and how it will check success. A longer task can have a saved plan behind that recap. Ask it to wait for your go-ahead.

“I'll check the spreadsheet” is vague. “I'll account for every source row and reconcile the totals after applying your agreed rules” gives you something assessable. For research, checks might include opening the cited sources and separating supported facts from assumptions.

Small, clear tasks can go straight through. Rephrasing one sentence usually needs neither a plan file nor an interview. Planning should grow with the importance and ambiguity of the task. Our approval rule is adapted from Superpowers, with this simple-task exception.

Review a small trial when the work matters

For important work, let the AI complete a small, representative part first. Have it run the checks and show you the sample before expanding. Include a difficult case in the sample: a refund in an expenses sheet, or an awkward file in an organization task.

Use that checkpoint to judge whether the approach matches what you meant. The AI can check a calculation; you decide whether the categories are useful. Once you approve, it can apply the approach more widely. Unimportant tasks can skip the sample.

During execution, it should fix objective errors within the agreed plan. If a new choice would change your preferences, scope, output, or cost, it should ask. This draws on GSD's distinction between repairs and decisions requiring input.

Look for evidence, then refine specifically

At completion, ask for the result, the checks actually performed, and anything still unresolved. A second agent can help review important work when available, provided it inspects the original brief and evidence. Agreement between two agents isn't a substitute for those checks.

If something is wrong, identify the mismatch and preserve what worked: “Keep the layout and totals. Separate business travel from personal travel, and ask me about transactions you can't distinguish.” The AI should update the relevant decisions and recheck the affected work.

For ongoing tasks, save the decisions and current progress somewhere the agent can read next time. Planning with Files provides one approach. You can begin with a short task note. Choose one useful task, get the questioning and approval process working, and build from there.

02 / Put it into practice

Plan a Tokyo trip around what you actually like

A fictional conversation and shortened itinerary to illustrate the method. This is not a researched travel recommendation.

Your flights and hotel are booked. You have four days in Tokyo and a few saved links. “Plan my trip” leaves the AI to decide what a good holiday means. A few useful questions can give it a much better brief.

Start with what you know

Help me plan four days in Tokyo around food, coffee, shopping, and time to wander. Here are my dates, hotel, and saved links.

Research Tabelog, r/JapanTravel, Japan Guide, and Time Out Tokyo. First interview me about my preferences, including how to use my saved links and whether to include other sources. Explain unfamiliar choices and help me decide.

Show me a brief plan, including how you'll check the itinerary, and wait for my go-ahead. Then research and build one day, check it, and show me. Wait for my approval before doing the other three.

Paste your details and links below the request. You don't need to work out every preference before starting; discovering them is part of the conversation.

Answer the questions that shape the trip

The AI reads what you supplied, then asks about the missing decisions. Here is part of that exchange:

AI: “How do you like spending a day? Any limits on walking or queues?”

You: “Start around 11. One main area each day, with room to wander. Walking is fine with café breaks. No queues longer than about 20 minutes.”

AI: “What kind of food and shopping? Any dietary restrictions or spending limits?”

You: “No dietary restrictions. Vintage clothes, small design shops, and good coffee. Up to ¥10,000 per person a day for food, except one special dinner where I'd go up to ¥20,000.”

AI: “Which saved places are must-dos? Are the named websites your priorities or the only sources? May I also check Japanese-language pages and venue and transport websites?”

You: “The vintage shops in Shimokitazawa are must-dos. The ramen link is just an idea. Those sites are priorities; the extra sources are fine.”

The saved ramen place now has to earn its place in the itinerary. A long queue could rule it out. The vintage shops have to fit, and the AI should ask before dropping them.

Approve the approach and try one day

The AI's recap could be:

I'll group your must-dos by area, use Tabelog for restaurant candidates, Reddit for traveler experiences, and Japan Guide and Time Out Tokyo for neighborhood and shopping ideas. I'll use venue and transport pages to check practical details.

I'll check opening days, estimated travel and food costs, and booking requirements. I'll flag unknowns, including queue lengths I can't predict. First I'll show you one relaxed day with an optional afternoon. Shall I start?

You approve. The AI researches, builds the first day, and checks it before showing you. You review whether it feels like your trip, then approve expansion or request a specific change.

For Reddit, ask it to read the accessible comments and replies in selected threads and report any coverage gaps. Repeated opinions are useful leads, not verified facts.

See your answers in the result

After you approve the checked first day, the AI completes the four-day itinerary. Here is an excerpt from that finished result. The venue names and lunch allowance below are fictional; the times illustrate your chosen pace.

Day 1 · Shimokitazawa

11:00 — Coffee and your saved shops. Have coffee near the station, then browse Elm Vintage and North Street Vintage, the two shops you marked as must-dos. There is no next booking to rush toward.

13:00 — Lunch. Try Corner Noodles, with a planning allowance of ¥2,500 per person. If the queue is over 20 minutes, switch to the backup, Station Kitchen. Your saved ramen place remains an optional swap.

14:30 onward — Leave it open. Wander, take another café break, or head back whenever you like. An extra shop is optional. Your special dinner is on day four, so there is no reservation to plan this afternoon around.

A researched version would link each stop to its supporting pages and include travel estimates, costs, booking tasks, and remaining uncertainties. This illustration contains no checked venues, routes, or availability.

Your answers are visible in the result: a late start, your saved shops included, a fallback for long queues, and an afternoon you can leave empty.

03 / Put it into practice

Two other ways to use the same method

The Tokyo example covers the full workflow. These shorter examples show what changes when the AI works on your computer or helps you decide what fits into a week.

Both examples are fictional illustrations. No personal files were accessed and no tasks were scheduled.

Organize a practice copy of Downloads

Start with: “Help me make Downloads easier to browse. Inspect the candidate folder I select, ask about useful categories, and propose a copied practice folder. Keep my originals.”

You select a candidate containing 12 files across several subfolders and allow inspection. The agent reads the folder, checks access, and asks:

“Should work documents stay together, or be grouped by file type? Should I rename files? Where should unclear items go? May I inspect document contents to help classify them?”

You choose purpose-based folders, permit content inspection, prefer existing filenames, and ask for a Review folder when the purpose is unclear. Age and size can help describe the clutter; neither establishes that something is disposable.

The agent proposes:

“I'll copy these 12 files into Downloads Practice. I'll try six representative files, including an unclear document and two receipts with the same filename. I'll avoid overwriting anything and record every old and new location. I'll check the file count, compare file contents with the originals, and confirm the move record accounts for the changes. After those checks, I'll show you the trial and wait for approval before organizing the other six.”

You approve. With file tools available, the agent creates the copy and folders. Before moving the six trial files, it finds Email attachments/receipt.pdf and Scans/receipt.pdf would both become Receipts/receipt.pdf. It proposes retaining one name and naming the other receipt-email-attachments.pdf, then waits for your choice. After you agree, it makes the moves. scan.pdf stays unchanged in Review because its purpose is uncertain.

The checked trial shows you actual folders and the move record. You approve the arrangement. The agent finishes and reports:

“Downloads Practice contains all 12 files: five in Receipts, three in Work, two in Installers, and two in Review. Every file matches its original contents. The move record covers all 12 files; no destination was overwritten. Your original folder is intact. Review contains scan.pdf and final-final.pdf, which still need your decisions.”

You now have a browsable result to judge, with a record that makes the changes traceable.

Turn an overloaded week into a doable plan

Your brain dump says: “Client deck due Thursday noon. Dentist Tuesday 3 p.m. Laundry. Renew passport sometime. Call Mum. Friday application deadline. I'm behind on everything.”

The AI asks about priorities, deadlines, remaining effort, and available time. You answer: the deck comes first and needs four hours; the application needs two hours; both deadlines are fixed; Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday each have two free hours. The dentist is already booked. The passport can wait.

It proposes a short plan, checks the six-hour limit and deadline order, and waits for approval. After you approve, the finished plan is:

Monday: deck outline and rough slides, two hours. Start laundry during a break.

Tuesday: keep the dentist appointment. Call Mum afterward if you have energy.

Wednesday: finish and check the deck, two hours; ready before Thursday noon.

Thursday: complete and submit the application, two hours; ready before Friday's deadline.

Passport renewal moves to next week's list. The plan stays in the conversation. Calendar entries and recurring jobs would need a separate request.

04 / Put it into practice

Research and delegate useful work

The basic workflow stays the same as the task changes. What changes is the information the agent needs, the tools it can use, and the evidence that would show the work is right.

Choose something worth handing over

With the right tools and access, useful requests can end in a working file, a researched decision, or a small piece of software. Give it an outcome you can inspect.

Task Useful outcome What needs checking
Spreadsheets An expenses workbook with categories, totals, and a review list. Every source row accounted for; calculations reconcile.
Writing A proposal or presentation built from your notes for a named audience. Claims, tone, and required points match your brief.
Job search Verified openings and application drafts tied to your experience. Roles are current; qualifications are not invented.
Creative work Several directions developed from your references and constraints. The choices reflect your taste and work in the intended format.
Small software A calculator, tracker, game, or page you can actually use. It opens, handles realistic inputs, and produces the intended result.

Give research a purpose and a search plan

“Research this business idea” can produce a polished report that never answers your actual decision. Start with what you need to decide: whether to interview potential customers, test a price, or spend a month building something.

Name the websites you care about, then have the AI ask whether they are priorities or the only permitted sources. Let it propose a search method before the main research: which questions to investigate, where to look, relevant languages and dates, and what would count as useful evidence. Approve that approach along with the output you want.

For a business idea, you might want competitor product pages for existing offers, customer discussions for recurring frustrations, and interviews you provide for people's actual workarounds. Each source answers a different question. A popular complaint does not establish that people will pay for your solution.

For Reddit or another discussion site, define a manageable set of threads and ask it to inspect accessible comments and replies. “Read all the comments” needs a boundary. Have it report what it covered, what it could not load, recurring views, and disagreement. If it counts a theme, it should say whether it counted comments, unique authors, or threads. Repeated or copied claims are not independent confirmation.

Discord and other logged-in communities need an accessible route. Provide specific channels, links, or an export you are allowed to share. If the agent cannot access them, it should say so. An inaccessible conversation is not evidence it has read.

Ask for a conclusion that distinguishes supported facts, reported experiences, and the agent's own inference. The important claims should link to the pages that support them, with dates where freshness matters. “No reliable evidence found” is a useful result when it is accurate. The research prompt puts this into one request.

Give agents roles when the work benefits

For everyday work, begin with an available general-purpose model in the subscription you already use. For difficult planning or review, consider a stronger available reasoning option; for straightforward extraction or repetitive formatting, a lighter option may be enough. Choose according to the task, account limits, and observed results. A model name or maximum effort setting does not guarantee correctness.

A subagent is another agent given a bounded piece of the work. It can help when tasks are independent: one investigates competing products, another reads customer discussions, and a reviewer checks the conclusions against the sources. The lead combines their findings and resolves inconsistencies.

Give each worker a question, relevant context, a clear deliverable, and a boundary on what it may change. Give a reviewer the original brief and underlying evidence. Asking several agents whether an answer “looks good” is a weak check if they never inspect the sources or calculations. This adapts the separation of implementation and review in Superpowers, while keeping the approval rules from this guide.

Use the Codex or Claude setup section for the models and agent features your account actually exposes. Keep workers within one provider to start. Before adding parallel work, have the agent explain why it helps and how it fits your usage budget.

Turn a useful task into recurring work

A Gmail morning briefing is a good candidate once a manual run gives you something you would actually read. Define the relevant inbox or labels, time window, what matters, where the result should appear, and the time zone. Ask it to distinguish messages needing a decision from background information, include links to the messages, and report incomplete access.

For example, your agreed format might be three sections: decisions needed, deadlines explicitly stated in messages, and useful updates. Ask for the message date beside anything time-sensitive. The agent should not invent deadlines or treat every unread message as urgent.

Have it produce one briefing, check its coverage against the agreed scope, and let you review the result. After approval, schedule future runs with the same rules. Keep actions such as replying, sending, archiving, or deleting outside a read-only briefing's scope unless you authorize them.

Before relying on the schedule, check where execution happens, which connections are available there, and what happens if a run fails. A reminder to read your email and an agent that reads it and produces a briefing are different tasks. Use a short test schedule, inspect the result and run time, and check notifications on the device where you want them. The product-specific setup sections distinguish local and cloud execution.

Continue from your phone

For a computer-hosted task, the useful goal is to open the same task from your phone and send the next instruction to the computer. Use the supported connection flow for your product, then test it with a harmless practice file. Ask from the phone for a small edit and confirm on the computer that the file changed. Merely seeing chat history does not establish that the phone can control the local task.

Keep chat access and file access separate. A file saved on the computer does not automatically become an attachment you can open in the phone app. Ask the agent where it saved the result and what supported preview or sharing path is available. Some products can expose artifacts; that does not mean every local file is automatically available.

A computer-hosted agent needs its host available. Plugged in, awake, online, and connected are separate conditions. Follow the host availability checklist and your product's setup section. Cloud work has different requirements; confirm it can reach the inputs before assuming it can finish the computer's task.

Fix a mismatch without restarting everything

Describe what is wrong, what should replace it, and what must stay. “Keep the structure and sources. Make the recommendation reflect my budget, and ask before dropping a must-have” gives the agent a useful correction.

Have it update the relevant plan and recheck affected work. If it repeatedly fails, ask what evidence, access, or decision is missing. A saved note with the objective, agreed choices, progress, and unresolved issues makes resuming easier; it should not claim the task is complete merely because the chat is ending. This follows the continuity approach in Planning with Files.

Try one useful task

Choose something small enough to inspect: a practice folder, a list of obligations, or a short research decision. Use everyday mode, answer the questions that matter, and look at the finished result and its checks. Keep the parts that worked and make one specific correction if needed.

Save any preference you expect to reuse in your working instructions. You now have a starting point for the next task instead of rebuilding the whole conversation.

05 / Use it again

Copyable prompts for everyday work

Replace the brackets with your details. These are instructions to use in your own task; nothing is executed by reading this page. Start with the everyday version. Add a narrower prompt when it helps.

Everyday mode

Everyday mode
Help me finish [outcome]. Context and material: [details].

For small, clear, reversible work, proceed directly and check it. For substantial or ambiguous work, ask a few targeted questions to settle consequential preferences, then show a brief plan with actions and checks. Wait for my approval to start. If I name websites, ask whether they are priorities or exclusive. For important work, check a representative trial, show it, and wait for my approval before expanding. Fix objective failures within the approved scope yourself. Deliver the result, checks performed, and remaining gaps.

Thorough interview mode

Use this when you cannot yet describe a good result.

Thorough interview mode
Help me define and complete [outcome]. Context: [details]. Start by checking the material and access available to you. Interview me until the consequential preferences and decisions are settled: purpose, audience, priorities, constraints, source choices, output, acceptable actions, and what success would look like.

Group independent questions in adaptive rounds of up to ten; ten is not a total limit. Hold dependent questions until the relevant answers are known. Explain unfamiliar options and their tradeoffs, recommend an answer, then wait for my choice or explicit delegation. Do not treat uncertainty or silence as approval. Investigate discoverable facts yourself. When I name websites, always clarify whether they are priorities or exclusive.

Show a concise recap and a plan covering execution and verification; save the fuller plan if useful. Resolve consequential decisions before requesting approval to start. For important work, check a small representative trial and show its results; wait for my approval before expanding. Repair objective failures within scope automatically. If checks repeatedly fail or access is missing, report the gap instead of claiming success. Deliver the result with evidence and remaining uncertainties.

Ask for a concrete plan

Ask for a concrete plan
Using our agreed answers, show the intended result, output format, boundaries, actions, and specific checks. Name factual unknowns and how you will investigate them. Flag consequential decisions still needing my answer. Keep the recap short and make any fuller saved plan accessible. Wait for my approval before execution.

Correct one mismatch

Correct one mismatch
Keep [parts that work]. Change [specific mismatch] to [desired result] because [reason]. Ask if this introduces a consequential decision. Update the relevant plan and recheck the affected work. Preserve unrelated content and report what changed.

Set the research scope

Set the research scope
Research [question] for [decision], using [named websites]. First ask whether those sites are priorities or exclusive, and explain any proposed additions. Agree on the depth and useful output. Check current factual claims against suitable original sources. For community discussions, examine accessible comments and replies in a defined sample; report coverage gaps. Separate supported facts, reported experiences, preferences, and your inferences. Repeated claims or votes are leads, not verification. Link the evidence and identify what remains unknown.

Check a result

Check a result
Check this result against the original brief and agreed rules. Use the source material, files, calculations, or cited pages to test whether it works. Report checks actually performed, failures, and gaps you cannot verify. Repair objective failures within scope, then recheck. Ask before changes that alter an agreed decision. Stop repeated unsuccessful attempts and explain what is still unresolved. If this is our trial, show it and wait for my approval before expanding.

Set up recurring work

Set up recurring work
Help me set up [recurring task]. Clarify the schedule and time zone, inputs, output destination, allowed actions, and what to do when inputs or access are missing. Check whether this setup can run it and how I can inspect results or stop it. Show the plan and wait for approval. For consequential recurring work, complete one run, verify its coverage and accuracy, and show me the result. Wait for approval before scheduling future runs. Include checks that each future result is current and complete. A simple reminder can skip the trial.
06 / Use it again

Save your working preferences

Use standing instructions for how you want the AI to work: when it should ask questions, how it should plan, and when it needs your approval. Keep the details of a particular trip, spreadsheet, or project in that task's own plan.

Start with the text below. For Codex, the usual filename is AGENTS.md; for Claude Code, use CLAUDE.md. Follow the Codex or Claude section for placement and checking which file is loaded. These examples have not been installed on your computer.

Instructions to copy

Instructions to copy
Help me reach a useful finished result. For a small, clear, reversible task, proceed and make the relevant checks yourself.

For substantial work, inspect the available material and clarify the consequential preferences before acting. Ask independent questions together, up to ten per round; adapt follow-ups to my answers. Explain unfamiliar choices and tradeoffs, recommend an answer, and wait for my choice or explicit delegation. “I don't know” and silence are not permission to decide for me. Investigate facts you can discover. If I name research websites, ask whether they are priorities or the only permitted sources.

Once the decisions are settled, recap the result, output format, boundaries, planned actions, and checks. Identify factual unknowns and how you will investigate them. Save a fuller plan when useful. Wait for my approval before substantial execution.

For important work, agree on a representative small trial. Do the trial, run the checks, show me the result, and wait for approval before expanding. Simple or unimportant tasks do not need an artificial trial.

During approved work, repair objective errors within scope yourself. Ask before changing an agreed preference, goal, scope, output, cost, or consequence. Preserve unrelated work. Existing approval continues to apply; do not ask me to approve the same step again. If an action would delete originals, send, publish, spend money, or submit something, make sure I have authorized that action.

Finish with the result, the checks actually performed, and anything unresolved. Support important research claims with accessible evidence; report source gaps and distinguish facts from inference. Repetition is not verification. If checks repeatedly fail, stop retrying the same approach and explain the gap.

For ongoing work, keep agreed decisions, progress, and open questions in a concise task note that can be read when work resumes.

Let the AI update your instruction file

Open the folder where you want these preferences to apply, then copy this prompt. Choose the recommended defaults or have the AI ask about your preferences first. It merges your chosen rules into existing instructions, or creates the file if absent. You review the proposed change before it saves.

Let the AI update your instruction file
Help me save these working preferences in the right instruction file: AGENTS.md for Codex, or CLAUDE.md for Claude Code.

First ask: “Use the recommended defaults below, or personalize them first?” Explain that defaults are the quickest route; personalization adjusts how we work together. Recommend defaults unless I want changes, and wait for my choice or explicit delegation.

If I choose personalization, ask one short batch about:
- Question depth: a few targeted questions, or a thorough adaptive interview with up to ten per round.
- Approval checkpoints: before substantial work, or before every nontrivial change. Existing authorization still applies; do not ask me to approve the same step again.
- Response detail and tone: concise or detailed; straightforward, casual, or another preference.
- Where the rules apply: this selected folder, or personal defaults across tasks. Recommend the selected folder; a global change requires my explicit choice.
- Any preferences I already want to keep or add.

Explain unfamiliar options and their practical tradeoffs. Recommend an answer when useful, and wait for my answers or explicit delegation. Silence and uncertainty are not permission to choose. Adapt the preferences below to my choices before proposing the file change.

First identify the tool, selected folder, and instruction files that apply, including any overrides. If the tool or folder is unclear, ask. Explain where the proposed file would apply. Start with this folder; changing personal defaults across unrelated tasks requires my explicit choice.

Read existing instructions before proposing changes. Preserve unrelated rules and wording, merge equivalent preferences, and avoid duplicates. Explain any conflicts and ask how to resolve them. Create a file only if the selected target lacks one. If this prompt has been used before, update the existing working-preferences section instead of adding another copy. Do not copy this guide's examples, setup instructions, or task-specific details into the file.

Merge these preferences:

- For clear, small, reversible tasks, proceed and perform relevant checks.
- For substantial work, inspect available material and clarify consequential preferences first. Ask independent questions together, up to ten per round, then adapt follow-ups. Explain unfamiliar choices, recommend an option, and wait for my answer or explicit delegation. Investigate discoverable facts yourself. “I don't know” and silence are not permission to decide.
- When I name research websites, ask whether they are priorities or the only permitted sources.
- Before substantial execution, recap the desired result, format, boundaries, actions, unknowns, and verification plan; wait for my approval. Save a fuller task plan when useful.
- For important work, agree on a representative small trial, perform and check it, show the result, and wait for approval before expanding. Simple or unimportant work does not need an artificial trial.
- During approved work, fix objective errors within scope. Ask before changing agreed preferences, goals, scope, output, costs, or consequences. Preserve unrelated work and existing approvals. Make sure deletion, sending, publishing, spending, or submission is authorized.
- Finish with the result, checks actually performed, and unresolved issues. Support important research claims with accessible evidence, distinguish inference from fact, and do not treat repeated claims as verification. If checks repeatedly fail, change the approach or explain the gap.
- Keep ongoing decisions, progress, and open questions in a concise task note.

Show the target path and proposed diff before writing, then wait for my approval. Once approved, ensure the previous contents can be restored; before changing an existing file outside Git, save a backup and report its path. Preserve existing uncommitted work in Git. Merge the changes and verify that unrelated rules remain intact and no preferences are duplicated. Report the changed path and scope. Then help me test the behavior in a fresh task.

Save them once and check the behavior

Ask the agent to inspect existing instructions before adding this text. Merge compatible preferences and flag conflicts; do not replace a project's existing rules blindly. For ordinary chat apps, use their supported custom or project instructions when available, or paste the everyday prompt into the task.

After saving, start a fresh task in the intended folder. Ask which instruction files it loaded and where they apply, then try an ambiguous practice request such as “Help me organize this list.” Check whether it asks the relevant questions before committing to a substantial approach. A claim that it loaded the file is useful to investigate, but its behavior still needs checking.

These instructions are an original adaptation of the interview, planning, and execution approaches used in this guide. You do not need to install those frameworks to use the instructions. An interview skill or larger framework can be an optional next step if the simpler setup leaves a specific need unmet.

07 / Set up your tools

Set up Codex for work on your computer

Checked October 2, 2026 (Korea; October 1 UTC). Interfaces and account access change. These steps use a reviewed GitHub code snapshot and the installed desktop build's interface text; installation, phone pairing, and scheduled execution were not tested. Evidence and exact sources.

Get one useful task working

Use the account you already have. Start at the desktop App link in the Codex repository, follow the graphical download/setup offered for macOS or Windows, and sign in with your ChatGPT account. If your installed ChatGPT desktop app already provides Codex work, use that entry. A roughly $20 subscription or employer-paid account does not establish every model, tool, or remote feature; check what your signed-in workspace actually offers. An API key is a separate route, so do not buy API credits just to follow this guide.

On a Mac, use Finder to make a small practice folder. On Windows, use File Explorer. Put copies of a few ordinary files there, then select that folder for a local task in the app. Avoid starting with your whole home directory. The app can have several execution destinations; confirm that this task points to the intended computer and folder.

Paste:

Tell me which computer and folder this task uses, and what files you can access. List the practice files, then create a short inventory document in this folder. Open it for me and check that every listed file exists. Preserve the originals. If you lack access, explain what is missing.

The AI does the checking. You should be able to open the document and recognize its contents. That establishes the starting point for the Downloads example. A confident response alone does not establish file access.

Give it short standing instructions

For a folder you will reuse, use the instruction-file merge prompt. Ask Codex to merge the preferences into the selected folder's AGENTS.md, or create it if absent. Review its proposed diff before saving; keep stable preferences there and the current task's decisions in its plan.

Then ask:

Check the working directory and applicable instruction files. Show their paths and summarize the rules that affect this task. Tell me about overrides or instructions you could not load.

Placement matters. In the reviewed code snapshot, project instructions are collected along the project-root-to-working-directory path. Without a recognized project-root marker, automatic discovery considers only the working directory. Instructions somewhere above an ordinary nested folder are therefore not guaranteed to load. More specific files and override files can also matter. Instruction discovery code.

Personal defaults across tasks can live in the actual Codex home folder, but start with the one task folder. Ask the agent to identify its Codex home before requesting a global change. Keep work-specific instructions out of unrelated projects. Instructions guide behavior; they do not grant access or guarantee compliance.

Choose effort, then consider extra agents

Start with the app's default model. For a difficult decision or substantial review, choose a stronger available option and an appropriate reasoning level. For clear extraction or routine formatting, a lighter option may be enough. Check the actual picker and usage allowance; models and supported effort levels come from a filtered catalog. Model metadata code.

Treat the available model and effort options as choices to test on your task, not a proven ranking or subscription promise. A model name alone does not supply tools, original evidence, or independent verification.

For substantial work, you can ask:

If subagents are available, use one worker for each genuinely independent part and a reviewer who checks the original sources and finished output. Give them bounded assignments and separate file ownership. Tell me if model or role selection is restricted. Stay within my current account; ask before introducing paid services.

One agent is enough for simple tasks. Extra agents consume usage and require integration; they do not make an unchecked answer trustworthy. The facility exists in Codex's implementation, but its availability and selectable roles vary by environment.

Continue the task from your phone

In the inspected desktop build, open Settings → Connections → Control this Mac or Control this PC, then Add. Follow its pairing/authorization flow with the ChatGPT app on your phone. Use the same intended account/workspace. If these controls are missing, check app versions and workspace access; do not treat a GitHub code feature as proof that your account has it.

Keep the host connected and running. The inspected build offers Keep this Mac awake or Keep this PC awake for plugged-in operation while remote access is enabled. Check the setting yourself; it does not establish that a closed laptop lid will work.

Before relying on this, open the host's existing task from your phone and send a harmless follow-up: “Read the inventory and report its file count.” Confirm the response and host identity. This tests conversation continuity on your setup. One September 23 Windows report describes successful phone execution and a desktop setup failure. The dated report.

The files still live where the task saved them. A local pathname in chat does not automatically create a phone attachment. Ask for a supported preview or export and try opening it on the phone. Chat access and artifact access are separate checks.

Schedule work after one checked run

If scheduling is available, ask the agent to set up the same job only after you have checked a manual run. Specify timezone, frequency, output, data access, and what to do if a run fails. Review whether it runs locally or in a supported cloud destination and which permissions it uses.

Local scheduled work needs its host and required tools available. Cloud work has its own access; it does not automatically inherit desktop folders or apps. The inspected app has Scheduled tasks and Previous runs views, including local/cloud distinctions. Check an actual scheduled result before depending on the routine. Dated implementation notes and limits.

08 / Set up your tools

Set up Claude for work on your computer

Checked October 1, 2026. Start with your existing Claude account. A roughly $20 subscription or an employer login does not establish which agent features, models, or connectors you can use. Check the options actually available before buying anything extra.

Claude Code can work with files through the desktop app. You do not need to learn programming to give it a file task. Its name describes its original audience; your first exercise can be organizing copies of documents.

Start with one local folder

  1. Get the desktop app from Claude's download page if needed. Sign in with your existing account. Look for its Code workspace. Check the app version and your account's available features if it is missing. The exact current Mac and Windows menus were not independently verified for this guide.
  2. Start a session that runs on this computer and select a small practice folder. Choose local if the app distinguishes local and cloud environments. A cloud session cannot be assumed to see your Downloads folder. If the app offers only GitHub repositories, check its version, account access and environment selection; do not create a repository just to make this exercise work.
  3. Ask it to prove that it can read the folder before asking it to change anything:

Tell me the folder you are working in. List five filenames from it without changing anything. Report any access limitation.

  1. Compare that list with Finder or File Explorer. Then use the Downloads exercise with copied files and a record of what moved.

The release history confirms desktop integration; it does not settle every account's interface. If you already use the terminal, the optional shortcut claude --desktop opens the desktop app from the current directory in a supported recent version.

Save a few standing instructions

Use the instruction-file merge prompt. Ask Claude to merge the preferences into the selected folder's CLAUDE.md, or create it if absent. Review its proposed diff before saving. Keep it short: how you want substantial tasks clarified, when approval is needed, how originals should be preserved, and how results should be checked. The individual task's preferences belong in its plan.

Start a fresh session in that folder and ask:

Which instruction files have you loaded? Give their paths and summarize the rules you will follow. If you cannot confirm loading, say so, then read this folder's CLAUDE.md explicitly.

Claude supports project instruction files, but a wrapper or app host can affect what loads. The SDK configuration makes this dependency explicit. Do not assume a file applies to every ordinary Claude chat or every unrelated folder.

Choose roles before models

Start with one agent. For substantial independent work, try:

Give one worker the bounded research task and another the output check. Tell each the brief, allowed sources, boundaries and required evidence. Keep file ownership separate. Integrate their findings and report disagreements.

Use the strongest model you can access for difficult decisions or review when needed, and a lighter available model for clear extraction or formatting. Opus and Sonnet are configurable examples, not a universal ranking. Check the actual model used and your usage allowance; several workers consume more of it. A reviewer must inspect sources or outputs, not merely agree with another model. Real agent definitions specify a role, tools and model. Ask Claude to create or manage a reusable definition only when useful.

Test a Gmail briefing before scheduling it

Use your app's available Gmail connection, with the account and scope you intend. Employer policy may restrict it. Ask for one manual briefing: your time zone, reporting window, included labels, urgency criteria, message links, incomplete coverage and a prohibition on sending or changing mail. Confirm that it actually retrieved the intended messages.

Then ask:

Show the exact recurring prompt, time zone, execution location, Gmail connection, output location and failure behavior. Explain what must remain running. Run one test for review before enabling recurrence.

There are three different arrangements:

Arrangement What to establish
A session loop The session's process must be available. Check expiry and resume behavior; it is not an always-on service.
A local desktop schedule Confirm app-open, awake, network and sign-in requirements, including what happens after a missed run.
A hosted routine Confirm cloud execution and attach its Gmail connector there. Local files and locally configured tools are not automatically available.

A tool connected only on your computer cannot simply be attached to a cloud routine; connect Gmail in the routine's own environment. Do not substitute a loop for a dependable daily job without explaining its limits. Keep local work plugged in and awake as required, and test lid closure separately; plugging in alone does not prove availability. Inspect the first scheduled result for fresh coverage and successful delivery.

Continue the same task from your phone

Try native Remote Control first where your account offers it; release notes confirm desktop-hosted sessions. Enable it for the computer session, use its connection link or pairing route, and open that session on your phone. Send: “Summarize our agreed plan and the latest completed check.” Confirm that it is the same conversation before giving new work. Keep the host process, computer and network available.

Starting a cloud task from your phone is another execution environment. Happy is an optional community alternative requiring a local wrapper and pairing; it adds setup and does not automatically adopt every desktop conversation.

Finally, test the output itself. Ask Claude to present the finished file through an available attachment or artifact route and open it on your phone. Remote chat supports file features, but saving a file on your computer does not automatically make it a phone attachment. If only a local path appears, request a readable excerpt for now and open the full file on the computer.

Source details and verification gaps: Claude setup evidence.

09 / Set up your tools

Keep your computer available for local work

Use this for work that runs on your home computer. A cloud task has its own execution environment; keeping your laptop awake does not give that task access to local files.

For the first setup, leave the laptop plugged in, online, and with its lid open. The display can turn off while the system remains awake. Closing the lid is a separate behavior and needs a separately verified setup.

Choose the simplest supported setting

Start with your agent app's built-in keep-awake setting if it has one. The Codex setup describes the setting observed in the inspected app build and its conditions. For another app, inspect its current controls rather than assuming it has the same option.

On a Mac, the built-in caffeinate utility can prevent idle sleep for a duration or while a chosen process runs. It does not establish that closing the lid will keep the task running. You can ask an agent to set up a temporary, process-bound session instead of changing system behavior indefinitely. See Apple's implementation.

On Windows, inspect the plugged-in system sleep setting. If you already use PowerToys, its Awake utility also has timed and indefinite modes, with separate display behavior. Test the result with the screen locked: the reviewed implementation snapshot explicitly handles lock state, so a setting's name alone is not an end-to-end check of your device.

Ask for a setup you can verify

Help me keep this computer available for local agent work while plugged in at home. Inspect the current settings and recommend a setup that lets the display turn off while preventing idle system sleep. Keep the lock screen and normal battery behavior. Explain how to restore normal sleep, and wait for approval before changing settings. Afterward, verify the configuration and help me test a short task while the screen is locked. I'll keep the lid open.

For scheduled local work, confirm the host and agent are still available at the scheduled time. For phone access, test a real follow-up instruction after the computer has been idle. A successful configuration change and a successful remote or scheduled run are separate checks.

This guide has not changed your power settings or tested your devices.

10 / Optional worked example

Turn a bank export into an expenses workbook

Worked example with fictional transactions. The workbook described here is a proposed output, not a completed file.

Suppose you have a messy bank export and want to know where your money went. You do not need to design a spreadsheet first. Tell the agent the result you want, give it access to an exported copy you choose, and make it resolve the decisions that affect the totals before it changes anything.

For example, you say: “Turn my August transactions into a personal-expenses workbook. I want monthly totals and a list of charges I should review.” The agent can inspect the copy to learn its columns and date format. It should then ask a focused batch of questions: Which currency should the report use? Do transfers between your own accounts count as spending? Should refunds reduce the original category? Do you want possible duplicates removed automatically or merely flagged? If you do not know what a choice means, it should explain the effect on the report and recommend an answer. It waits for your choice or your explicit delegation of that decision.

Once those answers are settled, the agent gives you a short recap. For this example, suppose you agreed to keep uncertain charges included, flag possible duplicates, exclude confirmed transfers between your accounts, and subtract matched refunds from spending. The proposed workbook has the original rows, a categorized ledger, a monthly summary, and a review list. Its checks will account for every row and reconcile the summary to the source amounts. You approve that plan before it transforms the data. The saved plan records these decisions and any unresolved facts.

For an important report, ask it to process a small, varied sample first. A sample of only straightforward grocery purchases proves very little. This fictional eight-row sample has the cases that often break expense summaries:

ID Description Amount (USD) Proposed treatment
T01 Groceries −42.50 Spending
T02 Rent −900.00 Spending
T03 Café −5.00 Spending; check for duplicate
T04 Café −5.00 Spending; check for duplicate
T05 Bookshop purchase −25.00 Spending
T06 Bookshop partial refund +12.50 Reduce Bookshop spending if the match is confirmed
T07 Transfer to own savings −300.00 Cash leaving this account; exclude from spending if it is your own transfer
T08 SQ* Cedar −18.00 Spending, category needs review

The agent should keep both café rows while their status is uncertain. They could be duplicated records or two real purchases. It should also keep the $18 charge in the spending total while labeling its category “Needs review”; hiding an unknown charge would make the report look cleaner and less accurate.

Here is a check the agent can show beside this sample. For the illustration, suppose you have confirmed that T06 is a matched refund and T07 is a transfer to your own account. Purchases total $995.50 before the refund and $983.00 afterward. Net movement across these eight rows is −$1,283.00: net spending of $983.00 plus the $300 transfer. There are eight source rows and eight accounted-for rows. On your actual task, the agent must calculate the checks from your file and confirm how it represents credits and debits.

Now you review the sample, especially the two judgments that arithmetic cannot settle: whether T03 and T04 are separate purchases, and what “SQ* Cedar” is. You can leave those facts unresolved and approve keeping the charges included and flagged. If a calculation fails, the agent fixes it and shows the corrected sample. If your categories or report format need to change, it asks. Only after you approve the sample should it process the rest of an important export. A trivial formatting request can skip this trial.

At the end, ask for the workbook, a short explanation of the totals, and a visible review list. Useful evidence is concrete: source row count matches processed row count; amounts reconcile; transfers and refunds follow the agreed rules; suspected duplicates and unknown merchants remain visible. If a check cannot be completed, the agent says which one and why. “I checked it” by itself tells you nothing.

Copyable starting prompt

I want a personal-expenses workbook from a transaction export I will point you to. Work from a copy and preserve my original file. First inspect the copy only to understand its columns, date range, amount signs, and any obvious data problems. Then ask me the questions you need to settle my preferences and the decisions that could change the totals or output. Ask up to 10 independent questions per round; ask dependent follow-ups after my answers. If I am unsure, explain the options, recommend one, and wait for my choice or explicit delegation. Do not guess how I want transfers, refunds, ambiguous merchants, or possible duplicates treated.

Before transforming the export, show me a concise plan: intended workbook, categories and calculation rules, files you will use, how you will verify row coverage and totals, and what will be left for review. Wait for my approval. Treat this report as important: process a small, varied sample, including any refunds, transfers, ambiguous merchants, and possible duplicates you find. Check the sample against source rows and show me the result. Wait for my approval before processing the entire file. During execution, fix objective errors within the approved plan; ask me before changing my preferences, the output, scope, or cost. Keep unresolved facts visible under our agreed treatment. In the final result, show the workbook, reconciliation checks, and unresolved items. If you cannot access the file or complete a check, say so plainly.

11 / Reference

Sources and further reading

This guide adapts practices from community GitHub projects for everyday tasks. It is original writing, not a promise that installing a framework makes an agent reliable. Repository activity and popularity helped identify sources; neither measures how well a workflow will work for you.

The main method

These four source files were checked on September 28, 2026. The links point to the versions used in the approved introduction.

Source What this guide takes from it
Matt Pocock's grilling skill Ask about decisions the user needs to make, group independent questions, investigate facts, and confirm shared understanding.
Superpowers brainstorming Clarify the intended result and obtain approval before substantial execution.
GSD execution Distinguish objective repairs from changes requiring a new decision, and check the result against acceptance criteria.
Planning with Files Save the plan, findings, and progress so ongoing work can resume.

Our adaptation permits clear, small tasks to proceed directly; uses question batches of up to ten; and requires approval after an important trial before expanding. Those choices combine the sources with the author's preferences. They are not all prescribed by any one repository.

For separate worker and reviewer roles, the guide also references Superpowers subagent execution, inspected during the September 18 review. The guide keeps decisions about unresolved user preferences with the user.

Product setup

The Codex and Claude sections state their individual research dates, using product repositories, relevant community implementations, and, for Codex, the installed desktop app's interface resources. Each section links its supporting evidence and states what was not tested. Current repository code is not proof that a feature is available in every account or app build.

We did not perform new installations, phone pairing, scheduled runs, or account connections for this guide. Follow the small access tests in the setup sections on your own devices. Product menus, models, limits, and connection behavior can change independently of the general workflow.

Optional deeper learning

Claude Code for Everyone is a further-learning option for nondevelopers, identified in the September source review. Its lessons were not adapted into this guide. Its course structure and current coverage should be checked before committing to it.

Framework installation is optional. Start with the copyable prompts and short working instructions. Add a tool or framework when you can name the specific problem it will solve.
